inputs.need:
I am the nurse lead for a 28-bed geriatric medicine ward in a 500-bed district hospital. Our delirium policy says every patient aged 65 or over is screened with the ward's 4-item rapid delirium screen (RDS-4) within 12 hours of arriving on the ward and then once every shift. When our practice development nurse spot-checked the nursing notes for one week in June, only about half of the expected screens were documented, and very few on night shifts. We also suspect that some documented screens are ticked without the patient being assessed.

Before we choose how to fix screening, we want to know exactly where and when it fails. I would like to run a 12-week prospective observational study on the ward: every day a research nurse would reconcile each patient's screening entries with the list of patients present on each shift, and on a sample of shifts she would watch whether the screen is actually done at the bedside. We want to describe the proportion of eligible patient-shifts with a completed screen, how this differs between day, evening and night shifts and between weekdays and weekends, and whether patients with dementia, hearing or vision loss, or in side rooms are screened less often. We also want to know how long it takes from a positive screen to a medical review, because a screen that nobody acts on is not much use.

We will not change ward practice during the observation period. The geriatricians are supportive, but the ward is busy, the research nurse has 0.4 FTE for 12 weeks, and we cannot add any paperwork for ward nurses. Many of our patients cannot consent for themselves, so we need a sensible approach to consent for observation.
inputs.constraints: The research nurse is funded at 0.4 FTE for 12 weeks only. No additional documentation or forms for ward nurses. Ward practice must not change during the observation period. Night observation is limited to two shifts a week.
localFacts: The geriatric medicine research ethics committee approved the observation protocol on 2026-08-26 (REB-GM-2026-058), with a waiver of consent for record reconciliation and verbal agreement or consultee advice for bedside observation.
The geriatric medicine division funded a research nurse at 0.4 FTE for 12 weeks from 5 October 2026 (letter GM-DIV-2026-11).
A one-week check of the nursing notes in June 2026 found 281 of 546 expected screens documented, including 31 of 182 on night shifts.
The ward admits about 14 patients a week, with a median length of stay of 11 days and average occupancy of 26 beds.

response.statement: Ward policy requires a 4-item rapid delirium screen within 12 hours of arrival and every shift for patients aged 65 or over, but a one-week check found about half of expected screens documented and very few at night. response.whatHurts: Undetected delirium leads to falls, longer stays, distress for families and discharge to care homes. Screens that are ticked without being done give false reassurance, and positive screens that are not acted on waste the effort of screening.

records.title: Completion of routine delirium screening on acute geriatric wards: a prospective observational study of 9,800 patient-shifts
records.authors: Moyo-Hartley P, Dahl-Onwuachi R, Quintero-Walsh E
records.abstract: Background: delirium screening is widely required but rarely measured as it happens. Methods: on four acute geriatric wards, research nurses reconciled nursing records with ward lists for every patient-shift over 10 weeks. Results: of 9,800 eligible patient-shifts, 58 percent had a completed screen. Completion was 71 percent on day shifts, 62 percent on evening shifts and 39 percent on night shifts, and it was 11 percentage points lower at weekends. Screens were completed within 12 hours of ward arrival for 64 percent of admissions. Conclusions: screening failed mainly at night and at weekends, and efforts to improve it should start from the points where the process fails.

records.title: Documented versus observed delirium screening: agreement between the nursing record and direct observation
records.abstract: We compared the nursing record with direct observation for 640 shifts on two geriatric wards. An observer shadowed the nurse responsible for each sampled patient and recorded whether the screening questions were asked. Screens documented in the record were observed in 83 percent of cases; in 17 percent a screen was documented but the questions were not asked, most often on night shifts and for patients who were asleep. Agreement was lowest for patients with severe hearing loss. The authors conclude that record review alone overestimates screening and recommend adding a sample of direct observation.

records.title: Electronic prompts and delirium screening completion in older inpatients: an interrupted time series
records.authors: Varga-Osei N, Lindqvist-Amadi J, Rourke-Tanaka S
records.abstract: We added a shift-start electronic prompt for delirium screening on three medical wards for older people and analysed weekly completion for 26 weeks before and 26 weeks after. Completion rose from 52 to 74 percent, with an immediate level change and no further trend. The increase was smallest on night shifts, from 31 to 45 percent. Time from a positive screen to medical review did not change. A concurrent staffing increase on one ward limits attribution, and nurses reported that the prompt often appeared while patients were asleep and was dismissed.

records.title: Missed delirium screening in patients with dementia or sensory impairment on geriatric wards
records.abstract: Using ward lists and nursing records for 1,450 admissions to three geriatric wards, we compared the proportion of patient-shifts with a completed delirium screen by dementia diagnosis and sensory impairment. Patients with a recorded dementia diagnosis had screens on 41 percent of shifts, compared with 66 percent for patients without dementia. Patients with severe hearing or vision loss had screens on 48 percent of shifts. Nurses' notes most often gave known confusion as the reason for not screening. Because delirium is more common in people with dementia, the groups least often screened are those at highest risk.

records.title: Nurse-reported barriers to delirium screening: time, perceived futility and uncertainty with dementia
records.authors: Harrow-Nkemelu B, Ostrowski-Fadipe A, Liang-Carvalho M
records.abstract: We asked 214 nurses on geriatric and general medical wards to rate barriers to routine delirium screening. The barriers rated most important were lack of time at the start of a shift (68 percent), the belief that screening changes nothing if doctors do not act (54 percent), uncertainty about screening patients with dementia (49 percent) and reluctance to wake sleeping patients at night (47 percent). Nurses who had received bedside training in the screen reported fewer barriers. The findings suggest that screening completion depends on what happens after a positive screen as well as on nurse workload.

records.title: Positive delirium screens and time to medical review on geriatric wards
records.abstract: We followed 386 positive delirium screens on two geriatric wards to the first documented medical review of the patient's mental state. Thirty-eight percent were reviewed within 24 hours, 29 percent between 24 and 72 hours, and 33 percent had no documented review before discharge or a later negative screen. Positive screens at night or at weekends waited longest. Review within 24 hours was more likely when the nurse escalated the result by phone rather than only recording it. The authors suggest measuring the step from screen to action alongside screening completion.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Studies on geriatric wards consistently report that screening completion is lowest at night and at weekends, and lowest for people with dementia or sensory loss, who are at the highest risk of delirium. Record review overstates screening because some documented screens were never performed. Positive screens often wait more than a day for medical review. A prompt raised completion in one time series but not at night and not the step to review. The pattern supports measuring completion per patient-shift with a sample of direct observation before choosing a fix.
response.gradeRationale: Consistent observational findings across several wards and methods for where screening fails; moderate certainty for the pattern, low for the effect of any single fix.
response.summary: Six retrieved records appraised; four source-derived claims with passages; overall certainty moderate.

response.reading: Screening sits between two pressures: the start of a shift, when nurses have least time, and the night, when waking a patient to screen feels wrong. The retrieved evidence places the failures at night, at weekends and in patients with dementia or sensory loss (claims c1 and c3), and shows that documentation overstates what was done (claim c2). Even a completed positive screen often waits a day for review (claim c4), which feeds the belief that screening is futile. Measuring each step, from list to screen to review, is the basis for any later change.

response.overview: Single-ward prospective observational study over 12 weeks from 5 October 2026: daily reconciliation of screening entries against ward lists for every eligible patient-shift, direct observation on a sample of shifts, and follow-up of every positive screen to medical review. Practice is not changed.
response.population: All patients aged 65 or over present on the ward during a nursing shift; patients receiving end-of-life care are excluded from the denominator as the policy exempts them.
response.exposure: Shift type (day, evening, night), weekday or weekend, dementia diagnosis, severe hearing or vision loss, and side-room care, recorded by the research nurse from the ward list and the notes.
response.procedures: Each weekday morning the research nurse reconciles the previous 24 hours (and weekends on Mondays) against the ward's shift lists. Each week she observes four day or evening shifts and two night shifts, following eight patients chosen by a fixed bed rota and recording whether the screening questions were asked. For every positive screen she records the time of the first documented medical review. If she sees an unrecognised delirium she informs the nurse in charge, and the event is recorded.

response.designSummary: Descriptive prospective observational study; patient-shift is the unit of analysis, with repeated shifts clustered within patients.
response.sampleSize: At an average occupancy of 26 patients, 12 weeks give about 6,550 eligible patient-shifts, about 2,180 of them at night. With completion near 55 percent and a design effect of about 3 for repeated shifts within patients, the overall estimate has a 95 percent confidence interval of about plus or minus 2 percentage points and the night-shift estimate about plus or minus 3.6. Seventy-two observed shifts with eight patients each give about 576 observed screening opportunities; if 83 percent of documented screens are confirmed, the confirmation proportion is estimated to about plus or minus 3 points. The sample is fixed by the funded 12 weeks, and these precisions are adequate for choosing where to intervene.
response.primaryAnalysis: Proportion of eligible patient-shifts with a completed screen, with 95 percent confidence intervals from a logistic model with generalised estimating equations and an exchangeable correlation within patients; completion reported by shift, weekday or weekend, dementia, sensory loss and side room.
response.secondaryAnalysis: Adjusted odds of completion for the six pre-specified factors in one GEE model; proportion of documented screens confirmed on observed shifts; time from positive screen to medical review with a cumulative incidence curve, treating discharge before review as a competing event.
response.missingData: Patient-shifts that cannot be reconciled because the list is missing are counted and reported; observed shifts that are cancelled are replaced on the next week's rota. No imputation.
response.multiplicity: One primary proportion; the six factors are pre-specified and reported with intervals as descriptive associations, not tested for significance.
response.software: R with the geepack package; analysis plan archived before the first shift.

response.summary: About 6,550 patient-shifts give the overall completion to about plus or minus 2 points and night shifts to about 3.6 points.

response.risks: Minimal: the study observes usual care. Risks are discomfort for nurses being observed, disturbance for patients during observation, and the observer seeing an unrecognised delirium; in that case she informs the nurse in charge and the event is recorded.
response.consent: Record reconciliation proceeds under the committee's waiver. Before bedside observation, patients with capacity give verbal agreement; for patients who lack capacity a family member or other consultee is asked for advice, and any sign of objection stops observation. Nurses are told which weeks include observation and may ask the observer to step away.
response.data: Data are recorded by bed, shift and study number; no names leave the ward; nurses are not identified in the dataset; files are kept on the hospital research drive for five years.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: people with dementia, sensory loss, limited English or in side rooms because of infection may be screened least. These groups are pre-specified in the analysis, interpreters are used for the verbal agreement, and results are reported separately so that improvement reaches them first.
response.effectiveness: Success is a clear map of where screening fails and whether positive screens lead to review, precise enough to choose the first change.
response.efficiency: Uses existing notes and one part-time research nurse; no paperwork for ward nurses.
response.costs: Research nurse time funded by the division for 12 weeks; no other costs.
response.grants: None needed; the findings could support a hospital improvement award for the chosen change.
response.partnerships: Ward nurses on each shift, the geriatricians, the practice development nurse and two carers of former patients with dementia from the hospital's carers' group.
response.rebPath: Approved by the geriatric medicine research ethics committee on 2026-08-26 (REB-GM-2026-058) with the consent model above; reporting follows STROBE.
response.limitations: One ward; observer effect; dementia status from documentation.
response.summary: Minimal-risk observation with a waiver for records, consultee advice for bedside observation, and equity groups pre-specified.

response.partnershipPlan: Two carers from the carers' group review the information sheet and the consultee process; a night nurse and a day nurse join the monthly study meeting; the geriatricians review the escalation findings.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the ward's compliments and complaints log from the last year is read for mentions of confusion or being woken.

store.title: Where delirium screening fails on a geriatric medicine ward: a 12-week prospective observational study
store.problem.rawNeed:
I am the nurse lead for a 28-bed geriatric medicine ward in a 500-bed district hospital. Our delirium policy says every patient aged 65 or over is screened with the ward's 4-item rapid delirium screen (RDS-4) within 12 hours of arriving on the ward and then once every shift. When our practice development nurse spot-checked the nursing notes for one week in June, only about half of the expected screens were documented, and very few on night shifts. We also suspect that some documented screens are ticked without the patient being assessed.

Before we choose how to fix screening, we want to know exactly where and when it fails. I would like to run a 12-week prospective observational study on the ward: every day a research nurse would reconcile each patient's screening entries with the list of patients present on each shift, and on a sample of shifts she would watch whether the screen is actually done at the bedside. We want to describe the proportion of eligible patient-shifts with a completed screen, how this differs between day, evening and night shifts and between weekdays and weekends, and whether patients with dementia, hearing or vision loss, or in side rooms are screened less often. We also want to know how long it takes from a positive screen to a medical review, because a screen that nobody acts on is not much use.

We will not change ward practice during the observation period. The geriatricians are supportive, but the ward is busy, the research nurse has 0.4 FTE for 12 weeks, and we cannot add any paperwork for ward nurses. Many of our patients cannot consent for themselves, so we need a sensible approach to consent for observation.
